prompt: Define a data race precisely (not just "two threads touch memory").
reveal: A **data race** is three things holding at once: two threads touch the **same** memory location, **at least one is writing**, and there is **no happens-before ordering** between them — nothing (no mutex, no atomic, no release/acquire pair) forces one access to be visible to the other. Drop any one of the three and it isn't a data race. In C++ a data race is **undefined behavior** — not "you read a stale value," but the whole program becomes meaningless, so the compiler is free to optimize as if it can't happen. **Tell:** not every *race condition* is a bug, but every *data race* is undefined behavior.

see.label: cppreference — C++ memory model (data race & UB)

prompt: Explain acquire vs release memory ordering as a pair. Why does a producer publishing a buffer need release, and the consumer need acquire?
reveal:
The gist: **release is "publish," acquire is "subscribe."** A release-store hands off everything the writer did before it; an acquire-load that reads that value receives all of it. They only work as a matched pair.

Precisely: a **release** on a store means every memory write the thread did *before* that store becomes visible to any other thread that later does an **acquire**-load reading the released value. An **acquire** on a load means once you observe that released value, you also observe everything that **happened-before** the release — the release-store *synchronizes-with* the acquire-load, creating a happens-before edge across the two threads.

So the producer writes the buffer, then does a **release**-store of the "ready" flag; the consumer does an **acquire**-load of the flag, and observing "ready" guarantees the buffer writes are already visible before it reads them.

**Tell:** without the pair, the flag can be seen *before* the data lands — the consumer reads a buffer the producer hasn't finished publishing.

prompt: Design a lock-free single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer. State: how you distinguish full from empty, which index uses which memory ordering, and why no lock is needed.

src.ref: §7.2.6 Writing a thread-safe queue without locks (single-producer/single-consumer)

reveal:
Gist: two counters — one owned by the producer, one by the consumer — chase each other around a fixed array; because each counter has exactly **one writer**, a single acquire/release pair is all the synchronization you need, no lock and no compare-and-swap.

**The layout:** a `head` and a `tail` counter that only ever increase (monotonic), and you take `counter & (capacity-1)` as the slot index — which is why **capacity is a power of two** (the mask replaces a modulo). **Empty** is `tail - head == 0`; **full** is `tail - head == capacity` — this design wastes **no** slot to tell the two apart, since the counters keep counting past the array size.

**Who does what, with which ordering:**
- Producer: **relaxed**-load its own `tail` (nobody else writes it), **acquire**-load `head` (to check there's room), write the slot, then **release**-store `tail + 1`.
- Consumer: **acquire**-load `tail` (to check there's data), **relaxed**-load its own `head`, read the slot, then **release**-store `head + 1`.

**Why no lock:** exactly one thread writes each index, so no two threads ever fight to update the same variable — there's nothing to serialize. Correctness comes purely from ordering: the producer's **release**-store of `tail` publishes the slot write, and the consumer's **acquire**-load of `tail` guarantees that slot write is visible before it reads. An approximate `size` reads both counters with two **relaxed** loads.

**Tell:** the "single writer per index" property is the whole trick — add a second producer and it collapses, forcing CAS on `tail`.

see.label: Rigtorp — A single-producer single-consumer lock-free queue

prompt: State the four Coffman conditions for deadlock and the single most common prevention discipline.
reveal:
Gist: a deadlock needs **four** things true at the same time; break **any one** and it can't form. These are the **Coffman conditions** (Coffman et al., 1971).

1. **Mutual exclusion** — a resource is held by at most one thread at a time.
2. **Hold-and-wait** — a thread holds one resource while waiting for another.
3. **No preemption** — a resource can't be forcibly taken away; the holder must release it voluntarily.
4. **Circular wait** — a cycle of threads, each waiting on a resource the next one holds.

Because **all four** must hold simultaneously, you prevent deadlock by making any single one impossible. **The standard discipline** attacks circular wait: impose a **global lock ordering** — every thread acquires lock A before lock B, everywhere, so a waiting cycle can never close.

**Tell:** if you can name a fixed order for all your locks and everyone obeys it, circular wait is structurally impossible.

prompt: What is false sharing, why does it wreck multithreaded performance, and how do you fix it?
reveal:
Gist: two threads write to two *different* variables that happen to sit on the **same cache line**, so the hardware treats them as shared data even though your program doesn't — and it silently kills performance.

Why it hurts: caches move memory in fixed **cache-line** chunks (typically **64 bytes**), not single variables. When two cores each write their own variable on one line, the **cache-coherence protocol** — the rule that keeps every core's cached copy consistent — must give one core exclusive ownership of the whole line for each write. So the line **ping-pongs** back and forth between the two cores' caches, one bouncing it away from the other on every write, as if they were contending for the same datum. They aren't; they only collide *physically*.

**The fix:** pad or align each hot, per-thread variable onto its **own** cache line so no two threads share one — `alignas(64)` on the field, or explicit padding bytes between them.

**Tell:** per-thread counters that are slower with more threads, for no logical reason, smell like false sharing.

prompt: Concurrency vs parallelism in one line each — and can you have one without the other?
reveal: **Concurrency** = *structuring* a program as independently-progressing tasks — dealing with many things at once. **Parallelism** = *actually executing* multiple tasks at the same instant on multiple cores — doing many things at once. You can have **concurrency without parallelism**: one core interleaving tasks by rapidly switching between them (they make progress, but never truly simultaneously). **Tell:** concurrency is a *design* property; parallelism is a *runtime* one — design for concurrency and parallelism becomes possible the moment extra cores exist.

see.label: Cornell Virtual Workshop — Parallel programming roadmap

prompt: When is an atomic (lock-free) approach actually better than a mutex, and what is the hidden cost of lock-free code?

src.ref: §7.1.4 The pros and cons of lock-free data structures

reveal:
Gist: reach for **atomics** (lock-free code) when the shared work is tiny and blocking would cost more than the work itself — but pay for it in correctness, not just speed.

**When atomics win:** the critical section is a single small operation — a counter, an index, a flag — and either contention or the cost of *blocking and rescheduling* a thread would dominate. Because no thread ever **blocks** (goes to sleep waiting on a lock), you also dodge two classic mutex pathologies: **priority inversion** (a low-priority thread holding a lock stalls a high-priority one) and **lock convoying** (threads pile up single-file behind one contended lock).

**The hidden costs of lock-free:**
- **Correctness is much harder** — you must reason about **memory ordering** (which writes are visible when) and the **ABA problem** (a value that changed and changed back, fooling a compare-and-swap).
- **Progress guarantees are subtle:** *lock-free* (the system as a whole always makes progress) is **not** *wait-free* (every individual thread finishes in a bounded number of steps) — don't confuse them.
- **Contention still bites:** under heavy contention a shared atomic still bounces its cache line between cores.

**Tell:** for anything beyond a single word of state, a plain **mutex** is often the correct, readable default — lock-free is a scalpel, not a hammer.

prompt: Explain relaxed, acquire, release, and seq_cst memory ordering. Which pairs with which, and what does each guarantee?
reveal:
Gist: these four tags say **how much ordering** an atomic operation promises with the memory around it — from "none" up to "one global order everyone agrees on."

- **relaxed** — atomicity *only*: the operation itself is indivisible, but it imposes **no ordering** on surrounding reads and writes. Fine for a counter where you just need the final total to be right.
- **release** (on a store) — **publishes** everything the thread wrote *before* it.
- **acquire** (on a load) — **sees** everything published by the release it reads from. Release and acquire are a **pair**: a release-store *synchronizes-with* an acquire-load of the **same** variable, creating a happens-before edge between the threads. (Neither does anything alone — one publishes, the other must subscribe.)
- **seq_cst** ("sequentially consistent") — everything release/acquire gives, plus a single **global total order** that all `seq_cst` operations across all threads agree on. It's the **default** and the easiest to reason about, at some performance cost.

**The common error:** saying "acquire *before* release." The release **publishes** first; a **later** acquire-load is what observes it. Order it release-then-acquire, publisher before subscriber.

prompt: What is compare-and-swap, and why is it the foundation of lock-free programming?
reveal:
Gist: **compare-and-swap (CAS)** is one indivisible hardware step that says "if this location still holds the value I expect, replace it — otherwise tell me it changed." That built-in *change detection* is what makes lock-free code possible.

Precisely: CAS atomically checks whether a memory location still equals an **expected** value and, if so, stores a **new** value — all as a single uninterruptible operation. It's the foundation because it lets you update **optimistically** and *detect interference*: read the current value, compute the new one off to the side, then CAS it in. If the CAS **fails**, someone else changed the location in the meantime, so you **loop and retry** with the fresh value. That **read → modify → CAS → retry** loop is the basic skeleton of nearly every lock-free algorithm.

In C++ it comes in two forms: `compare_exchange_weak` may **fail spuriously** — report failure even when the value matched — which is cheaper on some architectures, so you put it **in a loop** where a retry costs nothing. `compare_exchange_strong` never fails spuriously, for when you're not already looping.

**Tell:** if a lock-free design has a `while` loop around a CAS, that loop *is* the concurrency control.

prompt: What is the ABA problem, when does it bite, and name two fixes.

src.ref: §7.3 Guideline: watch out for the ABA problem

reveal:
Gist: a compare-and-swap checks only *the value*, not *the history* — so if a value goes A → B → back to A while your thread was asleep, the CAS happily succeeds even though the world changed underneath it.

**The scenario:** a thread reads value **A**, gets descheduled, and meanwhile other threads change the location to **B** and then back to **A**. When the original thread wakes and runs its CAS, the value *matches* A, so the CAS **succeeds** — but the underlying state is not what it was. Typically a node was popped and **freed**, and its memory reused, so you're now splicing in a pointer to reclaimed memory.

**Where it bites:** lock-free **stacks and queues** that CAS on **pointers**, where a freed-and-recycled node can reappear at the same address.

**Two fixes:**
1. **Tagged / versioned pointer** — pack a counter alongside the pointer so *every* modification bumps the tag; a recycled address now carries a different tag, making the ABA distinguishable from a genuine no-change.
2. **Deferred reclamation** — **hazard pointers** or **epoch-based reclamation**, which delay freeing memory so it's never reused while another thread might still be referencing it. No reuse, no ABA.

**Tell:** "my CAS on a pointer succeeded but the node was freed and recycled" is the signature of ABA.

prompt: When do you use a mutex versus an atomic? What is the real cost of each?

src.ref: §5.2.1 The standard atomic types (atomic vs lock-based)

reveal:
Gist: use an **atomic** when the shared state is a single word you touch with one indivisible operation; use a **mutex** when several pieces of state must stay consistent together.

**Atomic** — an operation that is **indivisible** (no thread can observe it half-done) — fits when the shared state is one word and the update maps to a single hardware instruction: a counter increment, a flag, a pointer swap. **Mutex** ("mutual exclusion" lock) fits when you must keep **multiple** fields consistent, or the critical section is non-trivial — no pile of atomics makes a **multi-field invariant** safe, because another thread can slip in between two separate atomic updates.

**The real cost of each:**
- An **uncontended** mutex is cheap — essentially one atomic operation plus a branch. Under **contention** it costs a **syscall** (a call into the kernel) and a **context switch** (the OS parks one thread and runs another) — on the order of *tens of microseconds*.
- An atomic operation is always a handful of *nanoseconds* — but a **contended** atomic still bounces its cache line between cores, so "lock-free" is not "free."

**Tell:** single word, one instruction → atomic; an invariant spanning fields → mutex.

prompt: Why must a condition_variable wait be inside a loop, and why does it need a mutex at all?

src.ref: §4.1.1 Waiting for a condition with condition variables

reveal:
Gist: the **loop** is because a wait can wake up when it shouldn't; the **mutex** is because checking your condition and going to sleep must happen as one uninterruptible step.

**Why the loop** — `while (!pred()) cv.wait(lock)`, not a bare `if`: a **condition variable** (a signaling primitive threads sleep on until notified) can suffer a **spurious wakeup** — the OS wakes a waiter even though nobody notified — and another thread may **consume the condition** before this one runs. Either way, on waking you must **re-check the predicate**; the loop does exactly that.

**Why the mutex** — checking the predicate and beginning to sleep must be **atomic** relative to another thread changing the predicate and notifying. Without the lock you could test the condition (false), get **preempted**, miss the notify that fires in that gap, then sleep — forever. That's the **lost-wakeup** problem. Holding the lock across the test-and-sleep closes the gap. `wait()` cooperates by **releasing** the lock while it sleeps and **reacquiring** it before it returns, so the predicate re-check always runs under the lock.

**Tell:** `if` instead of `while` around `wait` is the classic bug — spurious wakeups will eventually bite it.

prompt: Design a thread-safe queue. What are the tricky parts beyond wrapping a mutex around std::queue?

src.ref: §6.2.2 A thread-safe queue using locks and condition variables

reveal:
Gist: bolting one mutex onto `std::queue` looks safe but leaves three real problems — a racy interface, no way to wait, and lost elements on exceptions.

**(1) The interface is racy.** `front()` and `pop()` as *separate* calls means another thread can pop in the gap between them, so you read one element and remove a different one. Fix: **combine** them into a single `pop` that returns the value (or writes it into a reference), atomic under the lock.

**(2) Blocking behavior.** A consumer facing an empty queue needs to *wait*, not spin or fail. Add a **condition variable** (a primitive threads sleep on until notified) and wake waiters on push — always with the predicate **loop** to survive spurious wakeups.

**(3) Exception safety.** If the value's **copy constructor throws** while `pop` is handing it back, you can **lose** that element — it's already been removed from the queue but never delivered. Returning by `shared_ptr`, or **moving** into an out-parameter, avoids the throwing copy.

**Going faster:** fine-grained versions use **separate head and tail mutexes** plus a **dummy node**, so a producer (touching tail) and a consumer (touching head) rarely contend on the same lock.

**Tell:** the giveaway that a queue wrapper is naive is a `front()` immediately followed by a `pop()`.

prompt: Why can a single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer be lock-free with only acquire/release, no CAS?

src.ref: §7.2.6 Writing a thread-safe queue without locks (single-producer/single-consumer)

reveal:
Gist: with exactly one producer and one consumer, each index has a **single writer**, so nobody ever competes to update the same variable — and compare-and-swap only exists to referee *competing* writers.

**The single-writer property:** the producer alone writes the `tail`; the consumer alone writes the `head`. No two threads ever try to update the same counter, so there is nothing to serialize — a plain atomic **load** and **store** suffice, no **CAS** (compare-and-swap, the atomic "replace-if-unchanged" used when writers contend) required.

**Correctness then comes purely from ordering.** The producer writes the slot, then does a **release**-store of `tail`; the consumer does an **acquire**-load of `tail`, which guarantees the slot write is visible before it reads. That one **release/acquire** pairing is the entire synchronization — publish, then subscribe.

**Tell:** add a **second producer** and the property breaks instantly — now two threads write `tail`, so you're forced back to a **CAS** loop to arbitrate them.

see.label: Rigtorp — A single-producer single-consumer lock-free queue

prompt: Outline a thread pool: what does the worker loop do, and how do you shut it down cleanly?
reveal:
Gist: a **thread pool** keeps a fixed set of worker threads pulling tasks off a shared queue; the whole design turns on running task code *outside* the lock and joining every thread on the way out.

**The worker loop:** wait on a **condition variable** (a primitive threads sleep on until signaled) until the task queue is non-empty *or* a stop flag is set; **pop** a task; then **run it outside the lock**. That last part is critical — never execute arbitrary user code while holding the queue mutex, or one slow task blocks every other worker from getting work.

**Submission:** wrap the caller's callable in a `packaged_task` (a callable bundled with a **future**, the handle you read a result from later) and return that future, so callers can retrieve both **results** and **exceptions**.

**Clean shutdown:** set an **atomic** stop flag, `notify_all` so *every* worker wakes and observes it, then **join** all threads in the destructor. Decide **explicitly** whether shutdown **drains** the remaining queued tasks or **discards** them. Use `jthread` (a self-joining thread) or an RAII joiner so that even an exception mid-construction can't **leak** a still-running thread.

**Tell:** running a task while holding the queue lock is the pool anti-pattern that serializes everything.

prompt: Why should you never call mutex.lock()/unlock() directly? Name the RAII wrappers and when each applies.
reveal: Because any early **return**, **break**, or thrown **exception** between `lock()` and `unlock()` skips the unlock — the mutex stays locked and the program deadlocks. **RAII** wrappers ("resource acquisition is initialization" — lock in the constructor, unlock in the destructor) release automatically as the scope unwinds, even on an exception. The four: **`std::lock_guard`** — simplest, locks on construction, no manual control; **`std::unique_lock`** — movable, deferrable, and manually unlockable, and it's the one `condition_variable::wait` requires; **`std::scoped_lock`** (C++17) — locks **multiple** mutexes at once and avoids deadlock by ordering them internally; **`std::shared_lock`** — the reader side of a `shared_mutex` (many readers, one writer). **Tell:** a raw `lock()` with no guard is a deadlock waiting for the first exception.

prompt: How would you implement std::function? What is type erasure and where is the cost?

src.ref: §9.1.2 A move-only function wrapper (function_wrapper, type erasure)

reveal:
Gist: **type erasure** hides an object's real static type behind a uniform interface, so one wrapper can hold *any* compatible callable — that's how `std::function` swallows lambdas, function pointers, and functors alike.

**How to implement it:** define an **abstract base** with a virtual call operator (plus virtual `clone`/`destroy` for copying and cleanup); wrap the concrete callable in a **templated derived** class that overrides those; and have `std::function` hold a **pointer to the base**. Calls dispatch **virtually** through that pointer, so the callable's concrete type is "erased" from the wrapper's signature — the caller sees only `void(Args...)`.

**Where the cost is:** a **heap allocation** for the derived object, unless the callable is small enough to fit the **small-buffer optimization** (storing it inline in the wrapper); an **indirect virtual call** on every invocation; and usually **no inlining**, since the compiler can't see through the virtual dispatch. That's why a raw lambda or a **template parameter** (which keeps the exact type, so it inlines) beats `std::function` in hot paths.

**Tell:** `std::function` in a latency-critical inner loop is a red flag — it buys runtime flexibility with an allocation, an indirect call, and a lost inline.

prompt: Why is fetch_add on an atomic different from load, add, store? What ordering do you want for a plain counter?

src.ref: §5.2.5 Operations on standard atomic integral types (fetch_add)

reveal: `fetch_add` is a **single indivisible read-modify-write** — read, add, and store fused into one uninterruptible instruction. Doing it as separate `load`, `add`, `store` is **three** steps, so two threads can both read the same value, each add one, and one increment is **lost**. For a plain statistics counter — where you only need the final total to be right and no *other* memory has to be ordered relative to the increment — **`memory_order_relaxed`** is enough, and it's the cheapest. **Tell:** upgrade to acquire/release only if that counter *also* publishes other data to another thread.

prompt: What actually happens during a context switch, and why is it expensive?
reveal:
Gist: a **context switch** is the OS swapping one thread off a core for another — and the visible cost (a microsecond of bookkeeping) is dwarfed by the *invisible* cost of the new thread running on cold hardware.

**The mechanics:** the kernel **saves** the current thread's register state — including the **program counter** (where it was executing) and **stack pointer** — into its task structure, picks another thread, and **restores** that thread's registers. If the new thread belongs to a **different process**, it also switches the **page tables** (the map from virtual to physical memory), which **flushes or tags the TLB** (the cache of those address translations).

**Why it's expensive:** the direct work is roughly a **microsecond**, but the **indirect** cost dominates. The incoming thread arrives with **cold caches** and a **cold branch predictor**, so its first thousands of instructions run slowly while the caches refill — a penalty that lands *after* the switch and doesn't show up as "switch time."

**Tell:** this is exactly why HFT systems **pin threads to cores** and **busy-spin** instead of blocking — they're avoiding the cache pollution far more than the switch itself.

prompt: When should a thread spin instead of blocking? What is the hybrid strategy?
reveal:
Gist: **spin** (loop checking, staying on the CPU) when the wait is shorter than the cost of going to sleep; **block** (hand the core back to the OS) when it isn't — and the hybrid does a little of each.

**Spin when** the expected wait is **shorter than a context switch** (roughly a microsecond) *and* you have a **dedicated core** — the typical case for a low-latency handoff between two pinned threads, where parking and rescheduling would cost more than the wait itself.

**Block when** the wait may be long, or cores are **oversubscribed** (more threads than cores). Spinning there burns a whole core doing nothing and starves other work that could run.

**The hybrid:** spin **briefly** — with a CPU **pause/yield** hint inside the loop, which eases pressure on the sibling **hyperthread** and cuts power — and if the condition still isn't met, **fall back to blocking** on a **futex** (a kernel-assisted wait) or a condition variable. C++20's `atomic::wait`/`notify` implements roughly this pattern.

**Tell:** spin only with a core to spare and a sub-microsecond wait; otherwise the hybrid protects you from wasting a core on a long wait.

prompt: Implement a copy-on-write string: what does it save, and why did the standard ban COW for std::string in C++11?

src.ref: Copy on Write — and the C++11 ban

reveal:
Gist: **copy-on-write (COW)** lets several string copies share one backing buffer and only duplicate it the instant someone **writes** — cheap for read-heavy copying, but the sharing turns toxic under threads, which is why C++11 outlawed it for `std::string`.

**What it saves and how:** keep the character buffer behind a **reference count**, and let copies just bump the count and alias the same buffer — no allocation, no character copy. You only pay when a copy is **mutated**: a `detach()` runs at the start of every mutating operation (and before handing out a **non-const reference** into the buffer), duplicating the buffer so writers don't disturb the sharers. For read-heavy workloads that copy strings a lot, that avoids most allocations.

**Why C++11 effectively banned it** — two concurrency-driven reasons:
1. **`operator[]` returning a non-const reference must conservatively `detach`** — the library can't tell whether you'll write through that reference, so it has to assume you might, which duplicates the buffer and **defeats the savings** on the very common indexing path. (C++11 also requires `operator[]` to be O(1), which an on-access copy violates.)
2. **The reference count must be atomic**, so **every** copy and every destruction becomes a **synchronized** operation. On modern multicore hardware that atomic bookkeeping costs more than just copying a short string outright — so multi-threaded programs paid a heavy price for a **single-threaded** optimization.

**Tell:** modern `std::string` uses the **small-string optimization** (short strings live inline in the object, no heap, no sharing) precisely because COW lost on threaded hardware.

see.label: alf-p-steinbach — Why COW was deemed ungood for std::string

prompt: Define happens-before and data race precisely. What makes a program undefined behavior?
reveal:
Gist: **happens-before** is the ordering that decides which memory effects one thread is guaranteed to see from another; a **data race** is exactly the absence of it where you needed it.

**Happens-before** is a **partial order** (some operations are ordered, some genuinely aren't). *Within* one thread it follows **program order** — earlier statements happen-before later ones. *Across* threads it's established only by **synchronization**: a **release**-store synchronizes-with an **acquire**-load that reads it; a mutex **unlock** with a later **lock**; a thread's **creation** with the start of the new thread, and a thread's end with a **join**.

**A data race** is two threads accessing the **same** memory location, **at least one writing**, with **no happens-before** relation between them. In C++ a data race is **undefined behavior** — and that means more than "you get a wrong value": the *entire program* is meaningless, so the compiler may optimize on the assumption a race **cannot** happen. That's what makes a program UB — a single unsynchronized racing access poisons the whole thing.

**Tell:** **atomics** — with *any* ordering, including `relaxed` — do **not** race, because atomic accesses to the same location are always ordered; the race only exists between *non-atomic*, unsynchronized accesses.

see.label: cppreference — C++ memory model (happens-before & data races)
